headline: Red October: US tech stocks tumbled last night on Alphabet's earnings shock, dragging your AI and tech holdings down — but the long-term case for your portfolio remains intact.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: Pilbara fell 4% today in a rough session for lithium. There's no fresh company-specific news — this looks like continued sector-wide pressure as lithium prices remain depressed and sentiment around EV demand stays cautious. The long-term story depends on the EV rollout picking up speed; that thesis hasn't changed, but patience is required.

movers.name: Global X AI ETF
movers.note: The AI ETF dropped 2.79% today, largely reflecting last night's heavy sell-off in US tech stocks. Alphabet's earnings miss and broader NASDAQ weakness (-2.86% last night) dragged AI-exposed holdings down. Nothing structurally broken here — this is the ETF doing exactly what it says on the tin: giving you exposure to AI, including the volatile swings.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: Take-Two slid 1.67% last night as the broader NASDAQ sold off. GTA 6 news remains active — Take-Two filed 16 Vice City trademarks three weeks before the expected GTA 6 launch, a positive signal. A viral 'watermark leak' was debunked by insiders. The GTA 6 launch catalyst is still the key thing to watch.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: Microsoft dropped 1.55% last night despite reporting strong quarterly results — Azure cloud revenue accelerated, beating expectations. The market reaction reflects broader tech caution after Alphabet's earnings shock, not any Microsoft-specific problem. Morningstar noted the question is now whether all the AI infrastructure spending starts converting to returns. The fundamentals here remain solid.

movers.name: Alphabet (Google)
movers.note: Alphabet had a brutal session last night — down 1.45% on the day but the real damage was done after earnings, with the stock losing over $475 billion in market value in what's being called its worst-ever day. Search revenue missed expectations and cash burn worsened, spooking investors who worry AI tools like ChatGPT are eating into Google's core search business. This is a genuine concern to watch, not just noise.

movers.name: Vanguard Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: VGE slipped 1.16% today, tracking weakness in emerging market equities. Ongoing tensions in the Middle East (attacks on ships through the Strait of Hormuz are at their highest since the war began) and global uncertainty are weighing on risk appetite in EM assets. No specific local catalyst.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market ETF
movers.note: VTS fell 0.69% today, reflecting last night's S&P 500 drop of 1.82% — the ASX-listed ETF tracks US equities and absorbs those moves. The sell-off was driven by Alphabet's earnings miss and broad tech weakness. Still in the green overall for you (+3.42%), so nothing to worry about.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: VDHG barely moved today, dipping just 0.25%. Its diversified mix of global and Australian assets cushioned the blow from last night's US tech weakness. This is the fund doing its job — smoothing out the bumps.

movers.name: DHHF
movers.note: DHHF was virtually flat today, down just 0.22%. Like VDHG, its broad diversification across global markets means single-day swings in any one sector don't hit hard. Essentially unchanged — no news, no drama.

watch_today.title: Alphabet (GOOG): Earnings shock — hold, don't panic
watch_today.detail: Google lost $475 billion in market value last night after search revenue missed expectations and cash burn worsened. The worry is real: AI tools are starting to eat into Google's core search advertising business. Your position is already down 9.5% overall. That said, Alphabet still has enormous resources, YouTube, cloud, and its own AI. For a long-term holder, selling now locks in a loss. Hold and monitor whether search market share continues to erode over the next few quarters — that's the real signal to watch.

watch_today.title: PLS.AX: Lithium pain continues — hold for the long game
watch_today.detail: Pilbara Minerals dropped another 4% today and is now down a painful 60.83% on your investment. There's no fresh bad news today — this is ongoing lithium sector weakness. The long-term bull case (EV adoption driving lithium demand) hasn't disappeared, but it's taking much longer to play out than most expected. If you believe in that thesis and can stomach the volatility, hold. Only revisit if you think the EV story is fundamentally broken.

watch_today.title: GXAI.AX: AI ETF dips with tech — long-term hold
watch_today.detail: The Global X AI ETF fell 2.79% today on the back of last night's NASDAQ rout. Down 15.23% overall on your position. The AI story remains one of the biggest structural trends of the decade, but valuations in AI stocks are high and earnings misses (like Alphabet's) can trigger sharp falls. If you're in this for 5+ years, sit tight — these dips are part of the ride.

watch_today.title: RBA rate decision coming next week — watch for mortgage relief signal
watch_today.detail: Westpac is predicting the RBA will hold rates next week, but the WSJ notes the RBA's messaging is raising questions about whether rates have peaked. PM Albanese publicly called rate hikes a 'blunt instrument', distancing Labor from the RBA. If the RBA signals cuts are coming, that's good for growth stocks and property. Keep an eye on Tuesday's decision.

watch_today.title: Middle East tensions pushing oil higher — inflation risk
watch_today.detail: Crude oil jumped 2.08% last night to $104/barrel. Ship attacks through the Strait of Hormuz in October hit their highest level since the Iran-Israel conflict began. Higher oil means higher fuel and transport costs globally, which can re-ignite inflation and complicate the RBA's path to rate cuts. Watch this space — it affects everything from petrol prices to your ETFs.

watch_today.title: MSFT: Azure strong, market overreacted — hold
watch_today.detail: Microsoft dropped 1.55% last night despite solid earnings — Azure cloud accelerated and beat forecasts. The sell-off was collateral damage from Alphabet's shock, not a Microsoft problem. Your position is up 17.78% overall. Nothing has changed with the long-term case here. Sit tight.

world.summary: A big week globally: the Iran conflict is rattling oil markets and shipping lanes, the US midterms are shaping up with a historic papal vote, and Poland is in a constitutional crisis. Plus a massive crypto hack and Alphabet's market meltdown.

stories.title: Iran conflict sends Strait of Hormuz ship attacks to record high
stories.why_it_matters: Attacks on ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz — the narrow waterway through which roughly 20% of the world's oil flows — hit their highest level in October since the US-Iran-Israel conflict began. This is directly linked to the crude oil price jumping over $104 a barrel last night (+2.08%). Gulf states are being warned to rethink their trillion-dollar defence setups. For everyday Australians, higher oil prices eventually feed into petrol prices and inflation, which makes it harder for the RBA to cut interest rates.

stories.title: Pope Leo XIV makes history as first pope to vote in a US election
stories.why_it_matters: Pope Leo XIV — the first American pope — cast a ballot in the US midterm elections, making history as the first pope ever to vote in a US general election. He did so as an American citizen exercising his right. The US midterms are heating up, with races like Maine's tight Senate contest drawing national attention amid concerns about affordability and Trump's influence. The pope's participation is being seen as a cultural and political moment, though he hasn't endorsed any candidate.

stories.title: Judge orders Trump administration to stop threatening election officials
stories.why_it_matters: A US federal judge has ordered the Trump administration to immediately stop threatening election officials with criminal charges — a significant legal check on executive power right before the midterms. Officials in several states had reportedly been warned they could face prosecution over how they conduct elections. The ruling reinforces judicial independence, but it also signals how politically charged the election environment in the US has become.

stories.title: Poland's constitutional crisis: Top court chief suspended, 'coup d'etat' declared
stories.why_it_matters: Poland is in a serious political stand-off: the country's President Nawrocki suspended the chief of the Constitutional Tribunal (the top court), and the court has responded by declaring it a 'coup d'état'. This is a direct clash between the president and the prime minister's government, raising fears about the rule of law in a key NATO and EU member. It's the kind of democratic backsliding that Europe has been trying to prevent, and it has implications for EU cohesion and stability.

stories.title: Billions in crypto frozen after suspected Binance hack
stories.why_it_matters: Crypto worth billions of dollars has been frozen following a suspected hack of Binance, one of the world's largest cryptocurrency exchanges. Authorities acted quickly to freeze the funds, but the breach raises fresh questions about the security of centralised crypto platforms. If you hold any crypto assets, this is a reminder of the custody risks — 'not your keys, not your coins' as the saying goes.

markets.summary: A rough night on Wall Street last night — the NASDAQ dropped nearly 3% and the S&P 500 fell 1.82%, both driven by Alphabet's massive earnings miss. The ASX held up reasonably well today, gaining 0.18%. Oil pushed higher on Middle East tensions while gold sold off sharply.

indicators.name: ASX 200
indicators.note: Quiet positive session for the ASX today despite the US carnage last night. Resources and domestic sectors provided some support.

indicators.name: S&P 500
indicators.note: Last night's session saw the S&P fall 1.82%, dragged down by tech after Alphabet's revenue miss.

indicators.name: NASDAQ Composite
indicators.note: The tech-heavy NASDAQ shed 2.86% last night — Alphabet's results and broader AI earnings concerns hit hard.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)
indicators.note: Oil jumped over 2% as Strait of Hormuz ship attacks hit a record high. Watch for petrol price flow-through.

indicators.name: Gold
indicators.note: Gold fell sharply by 3.29% last night — unusual for a risk-off session. Possible profit-taking after a strong run.

indicators.name: AUD/USD
indicators.note: The Aussie dollar was barely changed, holding just above 70 US cents.

politics.summary: A busy week in Australian politics: Labor is moving to ban AI data centres from suburbs, there's growing heat on the RBA ahead of next week's rate decision, and the government is defending its $10 billion EU trade deal against Coalition criticism.

stories.title: Labor to ban AI data centres from suburban Australia
stories.why_it_matters: Labor is planning to block AI data centres from being built in residential suburbs — a move aimed at protecting neighbourhoods from the noise, heat, and electricity demand these facilities generate. Industry operators are already warning the policy confusion is putting billions of dollars in investment at risk, with some projects potentially delayed or cancelled. If you're invested in AI infrastructure plays, this is the kind of regulatory risk that can affect returns — though the ban appears aimed at location, not the industry itself.

stories.title: RBA rate decision looming — Albanese calls hikes a 'blunt instrument'
stories.why_it_matters: The RBA meets next week, and Westpac is predicting rates will be held steady. But the WSJ is reporting the RBA's recent messaging is making markets question whether rates have genuinely peaked. PM Albanese publicly distanced Labor from the RBA, calling interest rate hikes a 'blunt instrument' — unusual political commentary on an independent central bank. For mortgage holders, the question is when, not if, cuts arrive. A rate hold next week is expected, but the language in the statement will matter.

stories.title: Ex-Treasury chief tells Chalmers: slash public service to reach surplus
stories.why_it_matters: A former Treasury secretary is publicly calling on Treasurer Chalmers to cut the public service significantly in order to return the federal budget to surplus. The government has been spending heavily and is under pressure from economists and the opposition to show fiscal discipline. Budget surplus matters because it gives the RBA more room to cut rates — a government running deficits while inflation is elevated puts upward pressure on borrowing costs for everyone.

stories.title: Albanese defends $10 billion EU trade deal amid Coalition criticism
stories.why_it_matters: PM Albanese is defending Australia's $10 billion trade deal with the European Union after the Coalition raised concerns about farm access provisions and climate clauses embedded in the agreement. The deal could open significant new markets for Australian farmers and exporters, but critics worry the climate-related conditions could disadvantage Australian agricultural producers. This is a significant trade policy moment — the EU is Australia's third-largest trading partner.

ai.summary: The big AI news today is a rare moment of industry unity: Anthropic, Google, Microsoft, and OpenAI have agreed to let websites opt out of AI training. Elsewhere, AI regulation debates are heating up in healthcare and politics.

stories.title: Big four AI labs agree to let websites opt out of AI training
stories.why_it_matters: Anthropic (makers of Claude), Google, Microsoft, and OpenAI have jointly agreed to honour a standard that lets website owners signal they don't want their content used to train AI models — similar to how websites block Google's search crawler. This is a significant voluntary commitment from the four biggest players in AI, and it gives publishers and content creators more control over their work. It won't fix everything, but it's a meaningful step toward an internet where AI and content creators can coexist.

stories.title: Senator Warren slams Trump's voluntary AI safety deal as not enough
stories.why_it_matters: Senator Elizabeth Warren publicly criticised the Trump administration's approach to AI safety — a voluntary deal with tech CEOs — calling it nowhere near enough and accusing Republicans of failing to do their jobs on regulation. The debate reflects a widening political divide: tech companies prefer voluntary commitments they can shape themselves, while Democrats are pushing for binding rules. For investors in AI stocks, looser regulation is generally seen as a short-term positive, but the lack of clear rules creates long-term uncertainty.

stories.title: FDA and CMS scrambling to regulate AI in clinical healthcare settings
stories.why_it_matters: US health regulators (the FDA and Medicare/Medicaid administrator CMS) are scrambling to keep pace as more US states push to trial AI tools in hospitals and clinical settings. The problem is that AI products in healthcare update constantly, making traditional 'approve once' regulation obsolete. Experts are calling for regulation that follows the product as it changes. This matters because healthcare AI is one of the biggest near-term commercial opportunities for the major tech companies — getting the regulatory framework right could accelerate or slow billions in revenue.

stories.title: TBC launches 'Mischief' — a new AI video model built on Wan 2.2
stories.why_it_matters: A new AI video model called 'Mischief' has launched, built on the Wan 2.2 architecture and developed using neuron-derived techniques — meaning it draws on insights from how biological brains process information. What it can actually do: generate high-quality AI video content. This is another entrant in the rapidly crowding AI video space, where tools are getting good enough to create short films, ads, and social content without traditional production. The pace of competition in AI video is accelerating.

sport.summary: NRL is in the off-season but there's plenty happening: end-of-season farewells, big transfer rumours, and the Rugby League World Cup is creating controversy. AFL had a big result with Geelong locking in a top-two finish, and Carlton scored a major coaching coup.

stories.title: Cronulla Sharks farewell departing players
stories.why_it_matters: The Cronulla Sharks held their end-of-season farewell for departing players, with emotional scenes reported. Fox Sports also covered the story of a veteran player eyeing a new deal with the Dragons after leaving the Sharks. One player quipped 'I was a garbo' before rugby league — a reminder of the journeys these players take. The off-season player movement is well underway.

stories.title: Walker certain to leave Roosters; Dearden shuts down Cowboys-Walker swap rumour
stories.why_it_matters: Luke Walker's departure from the Sydney Roosters is now confirmed — sources say 'it's done'. However, Cowboys halfback Tom Dearden shut down rumours of a Walker-Dearden swap, reaffirming his commitment to North Queensland and saying 'she's coming up' for the Cowboys. With Jake Walsh also joining transfer speculation, the NRL silly season is in full swing.

stories.title: Rugby League World Cup format slammed as England faces historic exit
stories.why_it_matters: England are on the brink of a historic early exit from the Rugby League World Cup, and former player Jon Wilkin has come out swinging, calling the tournament format 'fundamentally flawed'. England's shock poor form has put them in danger of not making the knockout stages — which would be a catastrophic result for the sport's global ambitions. The format criticism centres on how pool stage results are weighted.

stories.title: Geelong locks in top-two AFL finish with clinical win over Western Bulldogs
stories.why_it_matters: The Geelong Cats secured a top-two AFL finals finish with a clinical victory over the Western Bulldogs. A top-two finish means a double chance in finals — if you lose one game, you get another shot. The Cats are now firmly in premiership contention heading into the business end of the season.

stories.title: Carlton pulls off major coup as premiership-winning coach signs on
stories.why_it_matters: Carlton has landed a major off-season coup, signing a premiership-winning coach to their setup. The Blues have been trying to take the next step after a finals campaign, and adding proven winning experience at coaching level is exactly the kind of move that can shift a club's trajectory. The identity of the coach wasn't named in the headline data, but it's being described as a significant signing for the club.
